blocks.text: 1. Fine-Tuning

blocks.alt: Pretrained weights go through fine-tuning to produce a task-specific model

blocks.text: Pretraining, the previous topic, trained a model once on a large, general dataset. Fine-Tuning is the second stage, adapting a pretrained model to a specific task, explored throughout this topic.
It works by continuing training on a genuinely smaller, task-specific dataset, a genuinely essential second stage covered throughout the rest of this topic.
2. Recapping Why Sharing Matters
This connects back to why this genuinely enables sharing, already covered in Pretraining. A genuinely expensive pretrained model, already covered there, becomes a genuinely reusable starting point.
Fine-Tuning is genuinely how that reuse actually happens in practice, directly delivering the practical benefit already covered generally at the end of the previous topic.
3. Starting From Pretrained Weights

blocks.alt: Random initialization is compared against pretrained initialization

blocks.text: This connects back to general-purpose representations, already covered in Pretraining. Fine-Tuning genuinely starts from the pretrained model's own already-learned weights.

This happens rather than genuinely random initialization, already covered throughout the Weight Initialization module, giving Fine-Tuning a genuinely enormous head start compared to training entirely from scratch.

blocks.text: 4. Needing A Genuinely Smaller Dataset

blocks.alt: Pretraining uses massive data while fine-tuning uses small data

blocks.text: This connects back to the scale of pretraining data, already covered in Pretraining. Fine-Tuning genuinely needs far fewer examples than Pretraining did, already covered there.

This holds since the model already genuinely knows broad, general patterns before Fine-Tuning even begins, directly leveraging the general-purpose representations already covered in the previous section.
5. Lowering The Learning Rate

blocks.alt: Pretraining uses a higher learning rate while fine-tuning uses a lower one

blocks.text: A genuinely important, real practical detail connects back to Learning Rate, already covered throughout Gradient Descent. Fine-Tuning genuinely typically uses a genuinely much smaller learning rate than Pretraining did.
This genuinely careful, deliberate choice, already covered in this section, directly connects to a genuinely real risk explored further in the very next section of this topic.
6. Why A Smaller Learning Rate Genuinely Matters

This connects back to catastrophic forgetting, a genuinely real, honest risk. A genuinely large learning rate could genuinely destroy the valuable, already-learned representations already covered in Pretraining.
A genuinely smaller learning rate helps preserve that genuinely valuable prior knowledge, directly protecting the general-purpose representations already covered in Starting From Pretrained Weights.

blocks.alt: A pretrained body gets a new task-specific head added to produce an output

blocks.text: This connects back to adding a classification head, already covered in Encoder-Only Models. A genuinely new, task-specific output layer often gets added on top of the pretrained model.

This directly reuses that earlier idea, now specifically within the Fine-Tuning process itself, adapting the pretrained model's own general representations to a genuinely specific, concrete task output.

blocks.text: 8. Full Versus Partial Fine-Tuning

blocks.alt: Full fine-tuning updates all weights while partial fine-tuning updates some

blocks.text: A genuinely important, real design choice connects forward to Frozen Layers, covered in the very next topic of this module. Fine-Tuning can genuinely update every single weight, or genuinely only some of them.
This genuinely important choice, already covered in this section, is explored in complete depth in the very next topic, directly building on the tradeoffs already covered throughout this topic.
9. Recognizing When Fine-Tuning Is Genuinely The Right Approach

blocks.alt: Having a pretrained model points toward using fine-tuning

blocks.text: This connects back to genuinely having a specific, real downstream task and limited task-specific data. Fine-Tuning, already covered in this topic, directly leverages the pretrained model's own broad knowledge.
This connects back to Pretraining's own expensive cost, already covered in its own topic. Fine-Tuning, already covered, avoids genuinely repeating that expensive process from scratch.
10. Worked Example
The example below directly demonstrates Fine-Tuning's own use of a smaller learning rate compared to Pretraining, illustrating the concepts already covered throughout this topic.

code.content:
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.RandomState(42)
hidden_size = 8

pretrained_weights = rng.normal(size=(hidden_size, hidden_size)) * 0.02  # already covered as starting from pretrained weights

pretraining_learning_rate = 1e-3  # already covered as lowering the learning rate in this topic
finetuning_learning_rate = 1e-5    # genuinely much smaller

def simulate_update(weights, learning_rate, rng):
    gradient = rng.normal(size=weights.shape) * 0.1
    return weights - learning_rate * gradient

weights_after_pretraining_style_update = simulate_update(pretrained_weights.copy(), pretraining_learning_rate, rng)
weights_after_finetuning_style_update = simulate_update(pretrained_weights.copy(), finetuning_learning_rate, rng)

change_from_pretraining_rate = np.linalg.norm(weights_after_pretraining_style_update - pretrained_weights)
change_from_finetuning_rate = np.linalg.norm(weights_after_finetuning_style_update - pretrained_weights)

print(f"Weight change with pretraining-style learning rate: {change_from_pretraining_rate:.6f}")
print(f"Weight change with fine-tuning-style learning rate: {change_from_finetuning_rate:.6f}")
print("\nNotice the genuinely smaller fine-tuning learning rate, already covered in this topic, produces a genuinely much smaller change, helping avoid catastrophic forgetting")

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: Fine-Tuning adapts a pretrained model to a specific task through continued training.
It is the practical realization of why sharing expensive pretrained models matters.
It starts from pretrained weights, rather than random initialization.
It needs far fewer examples than Pretraining, leveraging already-learned general patterns.
It typically uses a much smaller learning rate than Pretraining did.
A smaller learning rate helps avoid catastrophic forgetting of valuable pretrained knowledge.
A new, task-specific output head often gets added on top of the pretrained model.
Fine-Tuning can update every weight, or only some, a choice explored further in the next topic.
Next up: Frozen Layers, a closer look at which weights actually get updated during Fine-Tuning.
